notes: FDA CDER Warning Letter MARCS-CMS 716822, dated September 9, 2025, signed George Tidmarsh (CDER Director); FDA reviewed https://directmeds.com in August 2025. ad_content = the three bulleted claims under 'The following claims concerning compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide products appear on your website:', verbatim, one per line. title: FDA consumer page on compounded GLP-1s (accurate disclosure language control)
ad_content:
FDA is aware that some patients and health care professionals may look to unapproved versions of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists) drugs, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, as an option for weight loss. This can be risky for patients, as unapproved versions do not undergo FDA’s review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed.
[…]
Compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug.
Patients should obtain a prescription from their doctor and fill the prescription at a state-licensed pharmacy.
Visit FDA’s BeSafeRx campaign for resources to safely buy prescription medicines online.
Talk to your doctor if you have questions about your medicines.
[…]
Look for these warning signs, including if a company:
makes claims such as the compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug
offers medicine at deep discounts or prices that seem too good to be true
sends medicine that looks different than what you’ve previously received at your local pharmacy or was pictured on their website, or arrives in packaging that is broken or damaged or lacks instructions for use
does not require a screening and prescription by a licensed doctor before providing medicine
does not have a licensed doctor available to answer questions after you receive your medication
[…]
A compounded drug might be appropriate if a patient’s medical need cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug, or the FDA-approved drug is not commercially available. However, compounded drugs are not FDA approved. This means the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.
[…]
Some of the adverse events are serious and some patients reported seeking medical attention for their symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation.
must_not_flag: compounded drugs are not FDA approved
This means the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.
unapproved versions do not undergo FDA’s review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed
Patients should obtain a prescription from their doctor and fill the prescription at a state-licensed pharmacy.
Compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug.
makes claims such as the compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug
does not require a screening and prescription by a licensed doctor before providing medicine
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation
notes: Real published text, verbatim excerpts (non-contiguous blocks joined with '[…]') from FDA's page 'FDA’s Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss' (Drug Alerts and Statements; 'Content current as of: 10/01/2026'; opened 2026-11-17). Blocks come from 'Understanding unapproved versions of these drugs', 'FDA recommendations for health care professionals and patients', 'Telehealth red flags for consumers', 'Concerns with compounded versions of these drugs', and 'Dosing concerns with compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide'. Chosen per scope change (no synthetic data): it is the disclosure language fda-001..005 lacked, and it is US-government public-domain text, so it can be stored verbatim. It is consumer guidance, not an ad. Hard negative: it quotes the prohibited 'same as an FDA-approved drug' idea and the 'prescription by a licensed doctor' gate only as warnings; a reviewer that keyword-matches would wrongly flag it. Not used: wegovy.com branded copy with ISI was opened and fits, but it is Novo Nordisk copyrighted text and was not reproduced at length.

notes: Provenance: official 'hims' YouTube channel, uploaded 2025-01-28; aired during Super Bowl LIX (Feb 9, 2025). Downloaded at 480p with yt-dlp; captions = uploader-provided English captions. notes: Provenance: official 'Ro' YouTube channel, uploaded 2026-01-28; Super Bowl LX spot. Captions = YouTube auto-captions (they render 'Ro' as 'row'; corrected in ad_content). Fine print read from a 1080p copy (480p copy kept as asset; fine print is barely legible at 480p). Labels by agent from captions+frames; needs human confirmation. Verdict is needs_review because the ad names a drug class ('GLP-1s', 'FDA approved GLP-1 options... in a pill') but no specific product, so whether 21 CFR 202.1 broadcast major-statement rules apply to Ro (a telehealth platform, not the manufacturer) is a legal judgment; benefits are in audio while risk info is on-screen only for ~5s. The knee/glucose graphics are qualified by an on-screen footnote ("In clinical trials, patients who lost weight saw lowered glucose levels and reported improvement in knee joint pain."); whether these are off-label for the specific products prescribed needs a reviewer with current labeling. Context: Managed Healthcare Executive noted "Williams does not refer to a particular GLP-1, which explains the lack of a disclaimer about side effects" (https://www.managedhealthcareexecutive.com/view/wegovy-uacr-test-spotlighted-in-the-health-oriented-super-bowl-ads). notes: Provenance: official 'Ro' YouTube channel, uploaded 2026-10-01. No YouTube captions were available; transcript produced locally with Whisper (mlx-community/whisper-small.en-mlx). ASR errors corrected: 'Rose Sparks' -> 'Ro Sparks' (matches on-screen brand), 'todalafil' -> 'tadalafil'. Fine print read from a 1080p copy. Labels by agent from captions+frames; needs human confirmation. On-screen timing: compounded/not-FDA-approved single-line super ~0-10.3s; 'Prescription treatment for men, if eligible.' ~10.3-14s; sublingual 'faster than pills' super ~16-21.5s; end card ~24.3-30s: 'Connect with a licensed provider online to see if you're eligible. For Important Safety Information, visit ro.co/safetyinfo' + 5-line paragraph incl. 'This is a compounded drug product. Compounded drugs ... are not FDA-approved and do not undergo FDA safety, effectiveness, or manufacturing review.' No risk statement (e.g., nitrate contraindication) appears in audio or on screen; only a URL reference. Context: Adweek describes Ro Sparks as Ro's compounded 'fast-acting erectile dysfunction pill' that is 'not approved by the FDA' (https://www.adweek.com/brand-marketing/megan-fox-is-the-ed-treatment-in-new-ro-sparks-campaign/). The 'active ingredient in Viagra' framing parallels the 'same active ingredient' claims FDA objected to in its Sept 9, 2025 warning letter to Hims & Hers (https://spectrumlocalnews.com/us/snplus/health/2025/09/16/fda-takes-aim-at-hims---hers--weight-loss-drugs-in-ad-blitz); no FDA action specific to this ad was found.

notes: Provenance: official 'Keeps' YouTube channel, uploaded 2018-12-10 (pre-dates the 2023 FTC Endorsement Guides revision). Captions = YouTube auto-captions. Labels by agent from captions+frames; needs human confirmation. Included as a compliant control. Borderline points a human should confirm: (1) consumer endorser testimonial with only 'Individual results may vary.' as a qualifier; (2) an unlabeled Rx-style pill bottle appears on the end card next to the OTC minoxidil box, with no risk information - acceptable only if the ad is treated as a service/brand ad that names no Rx drug.
